AUDIT_F1.charter: A durable, versioned, reloadable semantic-truth persistence layer for compiled/verified IR (rules/definitions), with full provenance, tenant isolation, and trust-status gating.

task1_genuineReloadReproduction.method: A fresh document (Section 6.02 Liens - a `MAX(MONEY $5,000,000, MULTIPLY(PERCENT 10, METRIC_REFERENCE Consolidated EBITDA))` nested capacity tree, one real `conditions[]` entry with an `EVENT_ACTIVE` boolean expression, and one real `exceptions[]` carve-out - a materially richer shape than the original Workstream H test, which only ever persists a bare MONEY leaf with empty conditions/exceptions) was run through the real, unmodified `runContractAnalysis` end-to-end with scripted discovery/compile callers. A brand-new `new PrismaClient()` instance (never `lib/prisma`'s shared singleton the orchestrator wrote through) then queried `semanticTruthRecord` directly.
task1_genuineReloadReproduction.result: PASSED. The fresh client's independent query returned exactly 1 RULE row whose `payload` deserializes to the full nested tree byte-for-byte: the outer MAX node's 2 operands (a MONEY leaf with `amount: 5000000`, and a MULTIPLY node whose own 2 operands are a PERCENT leaf `value: 10` and a METRIC_REFERENCE `metricName: "Consolidated EBITDA"`), `conditions[0].conditionType === "NO_DEFAULT"` with a real `EVENT_ACTIVE` expression and its description text, `exceptions[0].description` containing the real carve-out text, `provenance.documentId` matching the real uploaded Document row's id, and every required version/provenance column (irSchemaVersion, compilerAlgorithmVersion, candidateRef, analysisRunId matching the real run's own id, version 1) populated with real values, not placeholders.
task1_genuineReloadReproduction.conclusion: The prior claim ('the payload deserializes to the real compiled IRRule') is independently reconfirmed, and STRENGTHENED - the original Workstream H proof never exercised a nested expression tree, a real condition, or a real exception; this reproduction proves the JSON round-trip is faithful for the actually-complex case, not just a single MONEY leaf. No non-JSON-safe value (Date instance, class instance, Decimal) exists anywhere in the IRRule/IRDefinition type shape (`ir/types.ts` confirmed field-by-field: `amount` is a plain `number`, `OperativeLineageRef.asOfDate` is a plain ISO `string`, nothing is a `Date` object) so JSONB round-tripping cannot silently corrupt a compiled rule.

task2_tenantIsolation.dbLevelVerification: Read prisma/migrations/20260830154356_phase_3f1_6_rx_workstream_h_semantic_truth/migration.sql directly (not just the Prisma schema DSL): `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "semantic_truth_records_companyId_instrumentKey_kind_semanti_key" ON "semantic_truth_records"("companyId", "instrumentKey", "kind", "semanticObjectId")` - companyId is a genuine leading column of the real composite unique index, not merely an application-level filter convention.
task2_tenantIsolation.adversarialTest: Constructed two synthetic tenants and deliberately forced an IDENTICAL instrumentKey + kind + semanticObjectId value across both (an artificial worst case stronger than relying on computeRuleId's own companyId-salted hash to naturally avoid collision) via persistSemanticTruthForInstrument directly. Then attempted a RAW `prisma.semanticTruthRecord.create()` for tenant A with the identical (companyId, instrumentKey, kind, semanticObjectId) as an already-persisted row.
task2_tenantIsolation.result: PASSED. Both tenants' rows persisted as two independent rows despite the identical key triple (proving companyId genuinely participates in the constraint, not just documentation). Neither tenant's own `getAllSemanticTruthForInstrument` read ever returned the other tenant's row. Re-persisting tenant A's rule with a changed amount updated ONLY tenant A's row; tenant B's row (same instrumentKey+semanticObjectId) was verified completely untouched. The raw duplicate-key insert attempt for the SAME tenant genuinely threw `Prisma.PrismaClientKnownRequestError` with `code === "P2002"` - a real Postgres-level rejection, not an application-code convention that merely happens to always avoid the collision. A control insert for tenant B with a genuinely distinct semanticObjectId succeeded normally, confirming the constraint is scoped correctly (not accidentally over-broad, e.g. keyed on instrumentKey+kind+semanticObjectId alone without companyId).
task2_tenantIsolation.conclusion: Tenant isolation is enforced at the database schema level via a real composite unique index, independently confirmed by reading the actual migration SQL and by a direct adversarial constraint-violation attempt - not merely inferred from application code discipline.

task3_downstreamTrustGatingEnforcement.traceMethod: Repo-wide search (`grep -rn` across all .ts/.tsx, excluding node_modules and this recertification's own new test files) for every real call site of getTrustedSemanticTruth / getAllSemanticTruthForInstrument / getSemanticTruthForRun / any direct `prisma.semanticTruthRecord.*` access outside lib/contract-model/analysis/semantic-truth/**'s own definition.
task3_downstreamTrustGatingEnforcement.finding: The ONLY real call sites found anywhere in this codebase are: (1) lib/contract-model/analysis/orchestrator.ts's own write call to persistSemanticTruthForInstrument (the producer, not a trust-gated reader); (2) the barrel re-exports in lib/contract-model/analysis/{index,semantic-truth/index}.ts; and (3) test files (Workstream H's own tests/contract-model/semantic-truth-persistence.test.ts and this recertification's own new file). NO application code outside this module - no API route, no server action, no UI data-fetch, no report generator - currently calls getTrustedSemanticTruth or reads SemanticTruthRecord at all.
task3_downstreamTrustGatingEnforcement.gatingCorrectnessVerified: A dedicated adversarial test (`TRUST GATING TRACE`) persisted one COMPILED row (verification never ran) and one NOT_VERIFIED row (verification ran and explicitly returned NOT_VERIFIED) side-by-side and confirmed getTrustedSemanticTruth's own result set contains NEITHER of them (`trusted.length === 0`), while getAllSemanticTruthForInstrument correctly still surfaces both at their real, non-VERIFIED trustStatus for audit/review visibility. The mapping function `computeTrustStatus` itself was independently re-verified against every real SemanticVerificationStatus value plus the UNSUPPORTED-sufficiency-wins case, matching Workstream H's own unit-test coverage.
task3_downstreamTrustGatingEnforcement.conclusion: The trust-gating READ FUNCTION itself is genuinely, correctly implemented and enforced within the persistence layer's own API surface: no code path can retrieve a non-VERIFIED row through getTrustedSemanticTruth, the one function this module's own header comment designates as the sole authoritative 'current truth' read. HOWEVER, this recertification's own repo-wide trace found that, as of this recertification, NOTHING in the live product outside this module's own tests actually calls that function or reads this table at all - SemanticTruthRecord is currently a write-only sink from the rest of the application's perspective. This does not violate AUDIT-F1's literal charter text (a durable, versioned, reloadable persistence layer with trust-status gating - which is what was asked for and what exists, correctly), and it means there is currently no live consumer that COULD bypass the gating (the narrow question this recertification task posed has a clean, if slightly unsatisfying, answer: there is no real call site to trace a violation into, because there is no real call site at all). This is disclosed here as a material caveat for whichever future phase wires a live reader to this table: the gating logic is ready and correct, but its real-world value is entirely deferred pending that integration.

task4_versioningPrecision.test: A rule with a nested condition (IRRule -> conditions[0] -> description, three levels deep) was persisted, then re-persisted four times: (1) baseline (version 1); (2) ONLY the nested condition description changed - a genuine content change three levels deep, not just a top-level field; (3) the identical content again (no-op); (4) ONLY candidateRef changed (pure governance metadata, never part of the IR payload/contentHash) with the IR content held identical to step 2/3.
task4_versioningPrecision.result: PASSED on every step: step 2 bumped version 1->2 and the new payload's nested description matched exactly; step 3 left version at 2 and reported `unchanged: 1`; step 4 left version at 2 (correctly NOT bumped, since payload content was byte-identical to step 3) while the `candidateRef` COLUMN itself did update to the new value (confirming mutable governance metadata refreshes independently of the content-hash gate, exactly as designed). Exactly 1 row existed in the table across all four persists (idempotent by construction, never a duplicate).
task4_versioningPrecision.conclusion: The contentHash gate genuinely distinguishes 'IR content changed' (bumps version) from 'governance metadata changed but content did not' (updates its own column, no version bump) at arbitrary nesting depth, not merely at the top level the original Workstream H test exercised (which only ever varied `capacityExpression.amount` directly).

AUDIT_F1.dispositionRationale: Every element of the charter (durable, versioned, reloadable persistence; full provenance; tenant isolation; trust-status gating) was independently, adversarially re-verified against real Postgres with a materially richer test fixture than the original certification used, and held. The one caveat recorded (no live downstream consumer exists yet) is a scope observation, not a defect in the persistence layer's own guarantees - the charter asks for a layer WITH trust-status gating, which exists and is correctly enforced within its own read API; it does not ask for a specific downstream integration, and none was claimed to exist by 09/10's own disposition text either.

AUDIT_F2.charter: Atomic ownership/claim mechanism (real Postgres coordination, not process-local mutex); proven with real concurrent callers.

task1_independentReproduction.method: A fresh Promise.all harness, written from scratch (not copied from tests/contract-model/analysis-run-concurrency.test.ts), against a brand-new company/identity, at higher concurrency (20 callers service-level, 8 callers orchestrator-level) than the original 12/6.
task1_independentReproduction.result: PASSED. Exactly 1 STARTED and 19 ALREADY_RUNNING at the service level; exactly 1 STARTED_TO_COMPLETION and 7 SKIPPED_ALREADY_RUNNING at the orchestrator level; exactly 1 AnalysisRun row ever created for the identity in both cases.
task1_independentReproduction.conclusion: The primary atomic-claim guarantee (never more than one caller observes STARTED for a fresh identity) is independently reconfirmed, not merely re-run from the original test file.

task2_staleReclaimAttack.whatStaleMeans: STALE_RUNNING_THRESHOLD_MS = 30 minutes (lib/contract-model/analysis/service.ts), compared against the row's own `updatedAt` (Prisma's `@updatedAt`, refreshed by any `update`/`updateMany` call touching the row - in production, every `setAnalysisRunStage` call during a real run). A RUNNING row whose `updatedAt` is older than `now - 30min` is treated as abandoned and safely reclaimable via the same atomic `updateMany` CAS.
task2_staleReclaimAttack.positiveFinding_neverPermanentlyStuck: Directly tested: a row backdated 90 minutes stale was reclaimed cleanly by a genuinely-concurrent 15-caller race (exactly 1 STARTED, 14 ALREADY_RUNNING, all pointing at the same reclaimed row - stressing the updateMany fallback branch under real concurrency, which neither this phase's design doc nor its results doc ever did; the original test only ever raced ONE caller against a pre-backdated row). A row backdated a full 24 hours was also cleanly reclaimed by a single caller. A row backdated only 29 minutes (inside the window) was correctly NOT reclaimed. CONCLUSION: a RUNNING row can never become permanently stuck regardless of how long it has been abandoned - the specific worry this recertification task posed ('could a permanently-stuck RUNNING row block all future analysis of that document forever') is FALSE; it does not happen.
task2_staleReclaimAttack.raceWindowBetweenCreateAndUpdateMany: Directly tested with a mixed-wave harness (two waves of 10 concurrent callers fired back-to-back with no serialization point between them, so some callers land on the create() branch and others land on the updateMany() fallback branch, genuinely racing against each other in real time). Result: exactly 1 STARTED across all 20 callers, exactly 1 row ever created. Both `create()` and `updateMany()` compile to a single SQL statement each; Postgres's own row-level locking under READ COMMITTED serializes concurrent UPDATEs against the same row (a blocked UPDATE re-evaluates its own WHERE clause against the just-committed row state once unblocked, per documented Postgres semantics), so no window exists for two callers to both observe a matching precondition. CONCLUSION: the design doc's own claim that this is 'a real Postgres-level compare-and-swap, not a process-local mutex' is verified correct - no race window was found between the two branches.

NEW_GENUINE_DEFECT_FOUND.title: The stale-reclaim mechanism is safe against a run that ACTUALLY crashed, but provides NO fencing/lease-generation protection against a run that is merely SLOW (a false-positive staleness classification) - a reclaimed row's original owner can continue to silently overwrite the new owner's live state.
NEW_GENUINE_DEFECT_FOUND.reproduction: A dedicated adversarial test (`PRODUCTION RISK - ZOMBIE WRITER`) constructed the exact realistic scenario the 30-minute threshold's own documented rationale dismisses as not happening ('comfortably longer than any single real analysis run this codebase's own scripted/E2E timing has ever observed') but does not structurally prevent: (1) an 'old worker' legitimately starts a run and enters PER_INSTRUMENT_ANALYSIS; (2) it goes quiet for 45 minutes WITHOUT crashing (a single stage covering many instruments/real LLM latency at production document volumes is a realistic way for this to happen, since `setAnalysisRunStage` is only called at stage BOUNDARIES, not per-instrument or per-LLM-call - PER_INSTRUMENT_ANALYSIS is one single stage spanning the ENTIRE per-instrument loop, however many instruments and LLM round trips that loop contains); (3) a legitimate new trigger correctly reclaims the SAME row per the documented (and, per task 2 above, genuinely correct) stale-reclaim contract - `startedAt`/`currentStage`/`fatalError` are reset, `AnalysisRunIssue` rows are cleared, exactly as designed; (4) the new worker makes real, genuine progress (advances to STRUCTURAL_ANALYSIS); (5) the OLD worker - which was never actually dead, only slow, and is never informed that ownership was reassigned, and never re-checks - finishes its own (by-then-meaningless) view of its own stage and calls `completeAnalysisRun(runId, ...)` using the SAME `runId` (reclaiming a row never mints a new id or any other token the old worker's own in-flight call would fail against). This call SUCCEEDS UNCONDITIONALLY and overwrites the row to `status: COMPLETED` even though the new worker's real execution is still only at STRUCTURAL_ANALYSIS. (6) The new worker, unaware, later calls `failAnalysisRun` itself (a real error) and this ALSO succeeds unconditionally, again overwriting the row - to FAILED this time. The final persisted state is whichever writer happened to execute last, a function of scheduling luck, not of who legitimately still owns the run.
NEW_GENUINE_DEFECT_FOUND.rootCause: `setAnalysisRunStage`, `completeAnalysisRun`, and `failAnalysisRun` (lib/contract-model/analysis/service.ts) all write via a bare `prisma.analysisRun.update({ where: { id: runId }, ... })` - an unconditional write keyed on the row's own immutable primary key, with NO compare-and-swap against any claim-generation/lease token minted at claim time. `startOrResumeAnalysisRun` never returns, and no `AnalysisRun` column ever stores, any value that changes across a reclaim OTHER than the fields a legitimate new owner would itself want reset (startedAt/status/currentStage/fatalError) - there is nothing for a genuinely-still-alive prior owner's own later write to fail against. This is confirmed directly against the REAL, currently-deployed lib/contract-model/analysis/orchestrator.ts: every one of its 5 `setAnalysisRunStage` calls and its `completeAnalysisRun`/`failAnalysisRun` calls use exactly this pattern, with no ownership re-check anywhere between the initial claim and any of these later writes.
NEW_GENUINE_DEFECT_FOUND.severity: Real production risk, not theoretical. This defeats the specific 'downstream semantic/review state is not double-written' guarantee 11/12's own design and results docs claim was proven - that proof only ever covered the SIMULTANEOUS-claim scenario (two callers racing to START at the same instant), never the RECLAIM-after-apparent-staleness scenario, where the mechanism that makes reclaim safe against a genuinely-crashed process (no ownership check needed, because nothing is left alive to violate it) is exactly the mechanism that makes it UNSAFE against a merely-slow process (no ownership check exists, and something IS still alive to violate it). Given that PER_INSTRUMENT_ANALYSIS is a single, unsubdivided stage spanning the entire per-instrument loop (however many instruments/LLM calls it contains) with the 30-minute threshold's own documented justification resting on an empirical observation about current test-fixture timing rather than a structural guarantee about production document volumes, this is not a remote edge case - it is a real and disclosed-here-for-the-first-time production risk.
NEW_GENUINE_DEFECT_FOUND.notPreviouslyDisclosed: Neither 11-analysis-run-concurrency-design.json nor 12-analysis-run-concurrency-results.json discloses this gap anywhere; both documents' own 'requiredProofsAddressed'/'testEvidence' sections describe only the simultaneous-claim proof and the single-caller-against-a-pre-backdated-row stale-reclaim proof, never a reclaim-then-original-owner-still-writes scenario.

task3_noRaceInCreateUpdateManyWindow.result: CONFIRMED NO RACE (see task2's raceWindowBetweenCreateAndUpdateMany above for the mixed-wave adversarial test and the Postgres row-lock-serialization reasoning). Both statements are genuinely atomic SQL statements; the two-step protocol between them is safe because each concurrent caller's own single statement is independently serialized by Postgres, not because of any external coordination this codebase adds.

AUDIT_F2.dispositionRationale: The literal claim-time atomicity AUDIT-F2's charter asks for ("Atomic ownership/claim mechanism... proven with real concurrent callers") IS genuinely real and was independently reconfirmed under harder conditions than the original certification used (higher concurrency, a genuinely-raced stale-reclaim branch, a mixed create/updateMany wave). However, this recertification found a genuine, reproducible, previously-undisclosed defect in the SAME mechanism's reclaim path: no fencing/lease-generation token prevents a stale-but-not-actually-dead prior owner from continuing to write to the reclaimed run row, allowing exactly the kind of uncoordinated concurrent double-write on downstream AnalysisRun state (status/currentStage/reviewItemCount) that this audit finding's own remediation claims to have eliminated. This is a real production risk (not a hypothetical or a documented, accepted limitation) that was explicitly called out as worth checking carefully in this recertification's own instructions, and it was found to be real. Per this recertification's own charter ('If you find a genuine defect, disposition STILL_OPEN'), AUDIT-F2 is dispositioned STILL_OPEN pending a fencing mechanism (e.g. a claim-generation counter or lease token minted at claim time and required - via a conditional WHERE clause - on every subsequent write to the run row) that makes a reclaimed run's writes fail closed against its former, superseded owner.

summaryForCaller.AUDIT_F1: CERTIFIED_CLOSED - durability, versioning, full provenance/tree round-trip, tenant isolation (verified at the real DB constraint level), and trust-status gating (verified at the read-function level) all independently reconfirmed against real Postgres with harder test fixtures than the original certification. One disclosed caveat: no live production code path currently reads SemanticTruthRecord outside this module's own tests, so the gating's real-world value is deferred pending a future downstream-integration phase - this is a scope note, not a defect.
summaryForCaller.AUDIT_F2: STILL_OPEN - the core atomic claim-time CAS is genuinely correct and was stress-tested harder than the original certification (higher concurrency, a genuinely-raced stale-reclaim branch, a mixed create/updateMany-wave race) and held in every case. But this recertification found and reproduced a real, previously-undisclosed defect: reclaiming a 'stale' RUNNING row provides no protection if the presumed-dead prior owner was actually just slow (a realistic scenario given PER_INSTRUMENT_ANALYSIS is one unsubdivided stage over the whole per-instrument loop) - the prior owner can keep writing to the same runId with no fencing/lease check, silently corrupting the new owner's live run state. This is the real production risk the recertification task asked to check carefully for, and it is real.
